mcqs.question: A dynamic array grows its capacity by a fixed +10 elements every time it fills up, instead of doubling. What is the total copy cost across n pushes from empty?
options: O(n), same as doubling
O(n²), because resizes happen every 10 pushes and each copies a growing multiple of 10 elements
O(n log n), because resizes get proportionally less frequent
O(1), since each individual resize only copies 10 elements
mcqs.explanation: With fixed-size growth, a resize happens every 10 pushes, and the copy sizes climb linearly (10, 20, 30, ...) — summing that arithmetic series over n/10 resizes gives O(n²) total, not O(n). Doubling avoids this because the resize sizes form a geometric series that sums to O(n) instead.

mcqs.question: In the accounting-method framing where each push banks extra credits for a future resize, why do the credits banked since the last resize exactly cover the next one?
options: Because the surcharge is refunded before every resize
Because doubling means the number of pushes since the last resize equals the number of elements that resize needs to copy
Because resizes are scheduled at fixed time intervals, not based on capacity
Because the array never actually needs to copy old elements during a resize
mcqs.explanation: Doubling means a resize from size k to 2k happens after exactly k pushes since the previous resize (which was itself at size k) — so the k pushes' banked credits line up exactly with the k elements that need copying. This one-to-one correspondence is what makes the accounting method balance cleanly.

mcqs.question: Using the aggregate method, n pushes into a doubling dynamic array cost O(n) for the pushes themselves plus O(n) total for all resizes combined. What is the amortized cost per push?
options: O(n), the total divided by 1
O(log n), the number of resizes divided by n
O(n²), the total cost multiplied by itself
O(1) — total cost O(n) divided by n operations
mcqs.explanation: The aggregate method divides the grand total cost across the whole sequence by the number of operations: O(n) total work over n pushes gives O(1) amortized per push. Dividing by anything other than the operation count, or not dividing at all, misapplies the method.

mcqs.question: A real-time audio pipeline has a hard per-call latency budget. Why might it avoid relying on a dynamic array's amortized O(1) push in its hot path?
options: Amortized O(1) is only a theoretical bound and doesn't hold in real programs
Amortized O(1) guarantees average cost over a sequence, but any single call can still be the O(n) resize, which could blow the per-call budget
Dynamic arrays don't support amortized analysis at all
Worst-case O(1) and amortized O(1) always produce identical latency profiles
mcqs.explanation: Amortized bounds are about the sequence's total or average cost, not any individual call — the occasional O(n) resize is real and can land on the one call with no latency slack. A system needing a per-call guarantee should pre-allocate capacity to get worst-case O(1) instead, which is a genuinely stronger and different promise.

mcqs.question: You profile a dynamic array's push calls and see a latency spike exactly at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Does this contradict the claim that push is amortized O(1)?
options: Yes — an O(1) claim should mean every call is fast
No — amortized O(1) describes the average over a sequence; individual resize calls are expected to spike, and that's consistent with the claim
Yes, because the spikes should occur at every power of 3, not every power of 2
No, because the profiler is measuring the wrong metric
mcqs.explanation: Amortized O(1) never claimed every call is fast — it claims the total cost over the sequence is O(n), so the average is O(1). Spikes at the resize points are exactly what the theory predicts, not a violation of it; conflating 'amortized' with 'every call is fast' is the specific misreading this pitfall names.
